turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come, Mr. Iyer, shoes off please. Temperature is thirty-eight point three.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. I feel like a wet rag. Can we just finish this, I've been waiting.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one oh nine over seventy-seven. Pulse is ninety-four, uh sorry, eighty-eight, I misread the screen.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Weight, err, the scale jumped to fifty-eight, no, fifty-two kilos. Last time in March you were sixty-eight. Your last pressure was one-forty.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I know I've lost weight. The trip food was rubbish, I've overdone it with all that fried stuff.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, please sit. I'm Dr. Menon. What has brought you in today?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): My eyes have gone yellow. And the urine is dark, like tea. It's really annoying, I look ill in every photo.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can see you're tired. When did the yellow eyes start?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Since Diwali or after... actually the trip was after Diwali. Maybe ten days. I can't pin the date, don't ask me to.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): And I'm exhausted all day. Also I can't hear myself think with that construction outside, it's ridiculous.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry about the noise, they're fixing the drain. Tell me about the urine and how you've been feeling otherwise.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Urine is dark, umm cola type, every time. Whites of the eyes, my wife spotted it first. Stools are a bit pale too I think.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or pain in the tummy?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Feverish at night, yes, I wake up hot. Tummy is not exactly pain, more a heavy feeling on the right side.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you vomit, or any loose motions?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Vomited twice, the first two days. That's stopped. No loose motions.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any itching of the skin? Swelling in the feet?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Itching a little at night. Feet are fine, not swollen. Don't poke them, I'm ticklish.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the trip, did you take alcohol?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't drink, not even beer. The others were drinking, I wasn't. Full stop.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about the food? You said roadside stalls.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Dhabas, almost every night. Pani puri, and fish from a stall that looked dodgy now. Three friends are also down, yellow eyes same like me.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): That helps a lot. Which medicines are you on at the moment?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Crocin, the fever one. I took two tablets when I felt hot. And my sugar tablets, the white ones, metformine five hundred, morning and night.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Metformin five hundred, morning and night. Since when?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Since last winter, or the one before. I cannot remember which year they started it. Ask my wife, not me.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): There was also a water tablet, uh Lasiks, but I stopped it months ago. Cramps were bad.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to a medicine or to food?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Eyes are yellow, the whites especially. Tummy is soft, a little tender just under the right ribs, and the liver edge is just palpable. No rash on the skin.

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): This looks most like an acute hepatitis, quite possibly from that food, though the bloods have to confirm it. A stone blocking the bile duct is less likely, but I won't fully rule it out yet.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Wonderful. I have a client meeting tomorrow. This is the last thing I need.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll send liver blood tests and hepatitis serology today, from here. Please don't take any more Crocin till we see the reports, paracetamol is not kind to an angry liver.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Those two tablets only, I didn't even finish the strip. It was doing nothing anyway.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Rest at home, fluids, light food, no fried dhaba stuff, and no alcohol. If you turn very drowsy, or the vomiting comes back, come straight to casualty.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And my friends? They'll WhatsApp me all night otherwise.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ask them to see a doctor as well, same story. I'll see you back in one week with the reports. Reception will book the slot.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): One week. Alright. I just want to go and lie down.

spec.situation: Person with yellow eyes, dark urine and tiredness after eating at roadside stalls on a trip; others at the trip also ill; alcohol denied; liver blood tests and hepatitis serology planned.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
